title: What's the deal with blood types?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore blood types, starting with the failed history of blood transfusions (animal blood, Jean-Baptiste Denis, James Blundell's human transfusions, milk injections) and Karl Landsteiner's discovery of the A, B, O blood groups. They explain antigens and antibodies, universal donors and recipients, the Rh factor and its link to mother-fetus incompatibility, other blood group systems, secretor status, and the Bombay phenotype. They cover how blood types vary across populations and may relate to disease resistance, blood types in animals, a documented case of a blood type change, Peter D'Adamo's Blood Type Diet, Japanese blood type personality theory, and a listener mail story about Rudolph Diesel.

segments.title: Opening banter and blood type small talk
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Jerry's blood type, share that they don't know their blood types, and banter about birthdays and famous deaths before introducing the topic.

segments.title: Early blood transfusion history
segments.summary: Early beliefs about blood as a vital life force led to bloodletting and attempts at transfusion using animal blood. Jean-Baptiste Denis's animal-blood transfusions ended badly, leading to a French decree banning transfusions.

segments.title: James Blundell and human transfusions
segments.summary: British physician James Blundell invented a transfusion device and tried human-to-human transfusions, with four of ten patients surviving. The hosts note he lacked a way to prevent reactions.

segments.title: Milk transfusions detour
segments.summary: In the mid-nineteenth century, doctors in North America tried injecting milk (cow, goat, human) into patients, with dangerous results. Patients were also given morphine and whiskey.

segments.title: Karl Landsteiner discovers ABO groups
segments.summary: Landsteiner mixed blood samples from healthy people and observed clumping, identifying the A, B and O groups; he initially labeled them A, B and C. The hosts describe plasma and his modest quote about the findings.

segments.title: Antigens, antibodies and compatibility
segments.summary: Blood types are defined by antigens on red blood cells. A has A antigens and anti-B antibodies, B the reverse, AB has both, and O has neither. O is the universal donor and AB the universal recipient. The hosts cover the Red Cross donation chart and immune hemolytic anemia.

segments.title: Rh factor and mother-fetus incompatibility
segments.summary: The Rh factor is a protein antigen named after the rhesus monkey. Rh-negative mothers carrying Rh-positive babies can develop immune responses, a risk that is now treatable. Rh-positive is more common than negative.

segments.title: Other blood groups, secretors and blood type frequency
segments.summary: At least twenty-two blood group systems exist, including Diego, Kell and Duffy. Blood types were used in early paternity testing and are heritable. Secretor status and ABO frequencies by population are discussed.

segments.title: Blood types and disease, Bombay phenotype, and blood type changes
segments.summary: Blood types are linked to differing disease susceptibility, possibly due to historical epidemics. The Bombay phenotype is a rare type lacking H antigen. Researchers have explored enzymes that convert blood types, and a girl's blood type changed after a liver transplant.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off, mention the website and social channels.
